items.titel: Listen: What can we expect from Ukraine peace talks in Abu Dhabi?
items.anriss: EUobserver is proud to have an editorial partnership with Europod to co-publish the podcast series “Briefed” hosted by Léa Marchal. The podcast is available on all major platforms .

absaetze.t: Production: By Europod, in co-production with Sphera Network.
EUobserver is proud to have an editorial partnership with Europod to co-publish the podcast series “Briefed” hosted by Léa Marchal. The podcast is available on all major platforms.
Find the full transcript below:
Talks on peace in Ukraine are set to continue this week in Abu Dhabi. And this time, the EU appears to have found a way into the room. But what can actually be expected from these negotiations?

After a period of doubts, the EU will finally be present in Abu Dhabi. According to the commission’s spokesperson, Paula Pinho, EU representatives will actually take part in meetings. That’s a change. In February, when talks were held in Geneva, the Europeans were left waiting in the corridor.

And they were under pressure. Last week, Italian prime minister Giorgia Meloni complained about scattered initiatives from the Nordic countries or from the E3 group, which created a cacophony. She called for clarity on the EU’s place, as an entity, in these talks.

So who will represent the EU exactly? On the EU side, it will be the chief of staff of the commission president Ursula von der Leyen, Björn Seibert, and the foreign policy adviser to European Council president António Costa, Ana Maria Boura. Both are quite used to taking part in leaders-level discussions, and both know the issues well.
And at the national level, the three countries of the E3 group had already carved out a place for themselves: France, the United Kingdom and Germany will also be represented.

Behind this push, there is a bigger concern: Europeans want a say not only on peace in Ukraine, but on the future of Europe more broadly. And they now feel a sense or emergency: last week, US President Donald Trump spoke of a potential “big beautiful deal” with Russia, to use his words. A deal that wouldn’t only concern Ukraine, but Europe too.

His son-in-law, Jared Kushner, was even more specific and talked about a security architecture for Europe. That did not go down well. Europeans reacted straight away, saying they don’t need others deciding on their security, and certainly not behind their backs.

So what does “security architecture” mean? It’s very broad. It’s about finding arrangements to protect Europe that Vladimir Putin can live with. Last week, we were talking about the security guarantees Europeans want to offer Ukraine, including the possibility of French or British soldiers on Ukrainian soil. You can easily imagine that Russia doesn’t want that.

Remember: before invading Ukraine in 2022, Putin demanded that Nato withdraw all troops stationed in countries that joined the alliance after 1997.That means all of Eastern Europe, plus Sweden and Finland. In other words, the countries geographically closest to Russia.
So the presence of Nato or European troops in Ukraine surely will be a point of discussion.

For their part, Europeans say the only problem with Europe’s current security architecture is that Russia doesn’t respect its existing obligations. In other words: it’s not for us to prove our good faith and pull back any troops.

So what would it take for the Abu Dhabi talks to move towards an agreement, compared with previous rounds? One side will inevitably have to give way on certain issues: either on the occupied Ukrainian territories, or on Nato.

That’s what Trump hinted at in an interview yesterday. He said he was confident a deal was within reach, and that it would probably mean Ukraine ending up, in his words, in a different form from what it is today.
It’s not the first time he has floated this idea of Ukraine leaving Donbas and Crimea to Russia.

items.titel: Cyberattaque contre des frigos : la justice ouvre une enquête visant des membres d'un groupe iranien, la France demande des sanctions européennes
items.anriss: L'attaque était inédite en France. Dans la nuit du 11 au 12 octobre, plus de 700 sites de la grande distribution française ont été visés par une cyberattaque. Les paramètres de dégivrage de leurs systèmes de réfrigération ont été modifiés, …

absaetze.t: Un mois après l'attaque contre les systèmes de réfrigération de plus de 700 sites de la grande distribution en France, la justice a annoncé l'ouverture d'une information judiciaire visant plusieurs responsables d'un groupe lié aux Gardiens de la révolution iraniens. À la suite de ces révélations lundi 9 novembre, la France a convoqué l'ambassadeur iranien.

L'attaque était inédite en France. Dans la nuit du 11 au 12 octobre, plus de 700 sites de la grande distribution française ont été visés par une cyberattaque. Les paramètres de dégivrage de leurs systèmes de réfrigération ont été modifiés, faisant monter les températures et les laissant dans l'obligation de jeter d'importantes quantités de denrées alimentaires.

Près d'un mois après, lundi 9 novembre, la France l'a officiellement attribuée à l'Iran, estimant qu'elle avait été menée par Shahid Kaveh, une unité cyberoffensive affiliée au Centre électronique et cyber du Corps des Gardiens de la révolution iraniens.

Une information judiciaire a parallèlement été ouverte contre "le chef du groupe iranien Shahid Kaveh, unité cyber offensive affiliée au Centre électronique et cyber du Corps des Gardiens de la révolution (CGRI-CEC), contre ses deux adjoints et contre toute autre personne qui serait identifiée", détaille la procureure de Paris, dans un communiqué.
L'ambassadeur iranien convoqué

L'annonce a vivement fait réagir. "Je suis en mesure de confirmer que la responsabilité de cette attaque revient au corps des Gardiens de la révolution de la République islamique d'Iran", a déclaré le ministre des Affaires étrangères français, Jean-Noël Barrot, dénonçant "une attaque d'une ampleur inédite et d'une agressivité inédite". Confiée à l'Office anti-cybercriminalité et à la Direction générale de la sécurité intérieure (DGSI), l'enquête a révélé "un mode opératoire d'attaque caractéristique de cette unité, l'utilisation du farsi et des adresses IP renvoyant vers des terminaux localisés en Iran", précise la procureure de Paris, Laure Beccuau.

"Nous prendrons des sanctions à l'échelle européenne contre tous les responsables de cette attaque", a soutenu Jean-Noël Barrot. Le ministre a également annoncé la convocation de l'ambassadeur d'Iran en France "qui annonce avoir "convoqué lundi l'ambassadeur d'Iran en France "pour protester très vivement contre cet acte extrêmement grave". Par ailleurs, la France pourrait aller plus loin, selon le ministre. "Nous ne nous interdisons rien et que nous prendrons toutes mesures, y compris celles dont nous ne ferons pas état publiquement, jugées par nous-mêmes proportionnelles et nécessaires pour dissuader toute nouvelle attaque et sanctionner les auteurs de cette agression inacceptable", a-t-il assuré sur Franceinfo.
Les autres attaques n'ont pas encore été attribuées

L'information judiciaire a été ouverte pour "des chefs d'atteintes frauduleuses à un système de traitement automatisé de données en bande organisée et de dégradations par un moyen dangereux pour les personnes en bande organisée", détaille le parquet de Paris. Ces deux infractions sont "aggravées par la circonstance d'avoir été commises dans le but de servir une puissance étrangère, en l'espèce l'Iran, outre la participation à une association de malfaiteurs en vue de la préparation d'un crime", ajoute le communiqué.

La France n'est pas la seule à avoir été touchée. Dans la nuit du 1er au 2 novembre, plusieurs autres pays européens ont été visés par des cyberattaques similaires. Mais pour l'heure, les attaques n'ont pas encore été attribuées. "Nous avons le Conseil des affaires étrangères lundi prochain [le 16 novembre], nous aurons donc l'occasion d'en discuter, car ces cyberincidents qui se produisent en Europe, s'ils sont attribués, appellent également une réponse forte de notre part", a déclaré dans la foulée la cheffe de la diplomatie européenne, Kaja Kallas.

items.titel: Excédent commercial chinois: la barre des 1000 milliards de dollars dépassée
items.anriss: La Chine a franchi dès octobre la barre des 1 000 milliards de dollars d’excédent commercial avec un bond des exportations vers l'UE et les États-Unis de 35 % le mois dernier, portées par l’intelligence artificielle et la voiture …

absaetze.t: La Chine a franchi dès octobre la barre des 1 000 milliards de dollars d’excédent commercial avec un bond des exportations vers l'UE et les États-Unis de 35 % le mois dernier, portées par l’intelligence artificielle et la voiture électrique.
2 min Temps de lecture

Plus d’un milliard de dollars par jour : c’est ce que la Chine engrange, en moyenne, d’excédent commercial avec l’Union européenne depuis janvier 2026. Au total, 310 milliards de dollars sur dix mois, soit près de 29 % de plus que l’an dernier, malgré les efforts des 27 pays membres de l'Union européenne pour inverser la tendance.

Le commerce extérieur continue de s'imposer comme un moteur de l'économie chinoise, notamment grâce à l'explosion de la demande pour les produits liés à l'intelligence artificielle et dans le domaine de la voiture électrique.

Sur le seul mois d’octobre 2026, les exportations chinoises ont bondi de 35,2 % sur un an, à 412,3 milliards de dollars. Les importations ont elles aussi nettement augmenté (+41,6 %, à 307,1 milliards), mais sans permettre d'empêcher le creusement du déficit. Parmi les exportations, 54,58 milliards sont allés vers l'Union européenne en octobre, Les exportations chinoises vers les Etats-Unis ont elle aussi bondi en octobre, de 32,9 % à 46,4 milliards, malgré le contexte de guerre tarifaire lancée par le président américain Donald Trump. Celui-ci doit rencontrer son homologue chinois Xi Jinping en marge du sommet de l'Apec (Coopération économique pour l'Asie-Pacifique) la semaine prochaine à Shenzhen, dans le sud de la Chine. Une réunion tripartite avec le dirigeant russe Vladimir Poutine est également envisagée.

L'année dernière, en 2025, la barre des 1 000 milliards de dollars d'excédent commercial n'avait été atteinte qu'en novembre l'année dernière. Et l'excédent commercial s'était conclu sur un record de 1 200 milliards de dollars à la fin de l'année.

items.titel: Börsengang von Anthropic
items.anriss: Der KI-Gigant Anthropic will an die Börse. Und damit könnten Tausende Mitarbeiter und Investoren zu Millionären werden. In San Francisco, dem Konzernsitz, werden explodierende Häuserpreise befürchtet. Von G. Biesinger. [ mehr ]

absaetze.t: Der KI-Gigant Anthropic will an die Börse. Und damit könnten Tausende Mitarbeiter und Investoren zu Millionären werden. In San Francisco, dem Konzernsitz, werden explodierende Häuserpreise befürchtet.

Ursprünglich war erwartet worden, dass der KI-Konzern Anthropic in dieser Woche seine Roadshow vor dem Börsengang startet, also seine Pläne potenziellen Investoren präsentiert. Bis Monatsende sollte dann der Schritt an die Börse erfolgen. Doch nach dem Abrauschen der Tech-Werte an den Börsen, nach dem Sieg der Demokraten bei den Midterms, wird spekuliert, dass sich Anthropics Zeitplan verzögern könnte.

Denn potenzielle Investoren drängen bei Anthropic inzwischen auf eine deutlich niedrigere Bewertung. Statt der ursprünglich angepeilten Höchstbewertung von bis zu zwei Billionen Dollar rechnen Insider "nur" noch mit einer Bewertung um rund 1,2 Billionen Dollar. So oder so, der Goldrausch in San Francisco, wo Anthropic sitzt, wird kommen. Und er wird erhofft und gefürchtet. Denn die Preise für Häuser und Mieten könnten weiter in die Höhe getrieben werden.
Tausende werden zu Millionären

Anthropic ist der erste reine KI-Konzern, der mit Claude eins der weltweit renommierten großen Sprachmodelle entwickelt hat, und jetzt den Börsengang wagt. Sobald das Unternehmen an der Börse notiert ist, können Beschäftigte und Investoren ihren bislang nur auf dem Papier existierenden Reichtum in echtes Bargeld verwandeln.

Schon vor der Sperrfrist für den Aktienverkauf können sie Kredite aufnehmen. Entsprechend stellt sich die San Francisco Bay Area auf einen Goldrausch ein, wenn Tausende über Nacht zu Millionären werden.

Der Chefökonom der Stadt San Francisco, Ted Egan, sieht in Anthropics Schritt an die Börse einen Wendepunkt für die lokale Wirtschaft, wie ihn die Region seit dem Börsengang des Transportdienstleisters Uber 2019 nicht mehr erlebt habe. In den kommenden Monaten werde in San Francisco und der Bay Area ein enormes Vermögen geschaffen.

Und obwohl die Stadt Vermögen oder Einkünfte aus Aktienverkäufen nicht direkt besteuern kann, wird sie über den Immobilienhandel auf ihre Kosten kommen, erklärt Egan. Denn bei Immobilienverkäufen fällt eine Transaktionssteuer an, die die Verkäuferin oder der Verkäufer an die Stadt entrichtet. Bei hochpreisigen Immobilien, die für mehr als zehn Millionen Dollar verkauft werden, liegt dieser Satz bei 5,5 Prozent - ​​es geht also um beträchtliche Summen.
Preise USA-weit die höchsten

Das Immobilienunternehmen Red Fin Homes in San Francisco hat schon im September errechnet, dass die Immobilienpreise dort die derzeit höchsten in den ganzen USA sind. Laut der "San Francisco Association of Realtors" liegt der durchschnittliche Preis für ein Einfamilienhaus in San Francisco bei etwa drei Millionen Dollar - wobei sich die Nachfrage zunehmend auf das höhere Preissegment konzentriert, schildert Verbandsvertreter Jay Cheng im Sender ABC. Im Vergleich zwischen dem ersten Quartal 2025 und 2026 sei die Zahl der Verkäufe von Häusern im Wert von über fünf Millionen Dollar um 69 Prozent gestiegen.

Immobilienmakler wie Austin Klar beobachten steigendes Kaufinteresse bei gleichzeitig knappem Angebot. Die Situation sei so extrem wie seit vielen Jahren nicht mehr. Viele Verkäufer würden sich derzeit zurückhalten, weil sie nach dem Anthropic-Börsengang mit einer regelrechten Explosion der Preise rechnen und ihre Immobilien noch nicht auf den Markt bringen. Es gebe weniger Verkäuferinnen und Verkäufer, aber immer mehr Kaufinteressenten.
Menschen mit normalem Einkommen bleiben auf der Strecke

Bei dieser Preisspirale bleiben Menschen mit normalem Einkommen, die nicht in der lukrativen Tech-Branche arbeiten, natürlich auf der Strecke. Wegen des hohen Preisgefüges ist Bauen in San Francisco vergleichsweise teuer. Laut städtischen Vorgaben müssten bis zum Jahr 2031 rund 82.000 neue Wohnungen entstehen, doch die Stadt hinkt im Zeitplan hinterher.

Auch Sam Moss, Geschäftsführer der gemeinnützigen Wohnungsbaugesellschaft Mission Housing Development Corporation befürchtet, dass sich die Situation für Einwohnende mit Durchschnittsgehältern weiter verschärfen könnte. Es sei ohnehin schon traurig, dass die meisten Menschen sich gar kein Wohneigentum mehr leisten könnten.
Langsame Genehmigungsverfahren

Die Genehmigungsverfahren in San Francisco gelten als die langsamsten im ganzen Land. Das lokale System erlaubt es Anwohnern, Bauprojekte über Einsprüche und öffentliche Debatten jahrelang zu blockieren oder erheblich zu verkleinern, meist aus Sorge um den Charakter des Viertels.

Insofern sieht Sam Moss die politischen Entscheidungsträger auf kommunaler, Landes- und Bundeebene in der Pflicht: Es sei wohl einfacher, Softwareentwickler zu verteufeln, als Gesetze kritisch zu hinterfragen, die den Bau bezahlbarer Wohnungen in San Francisco über Generationen hinweg erschwert hätten.

items.titel: More computing power, more jobs? Denmark boosts its AI supercomputer
items.anriss: The 500 million DKK (€67 million) investment in Denmark’s AI supercomputer could help create businesses and jobs and enable public institutions to use AI securely, according to Tuesday’s announcement.

absaetze.t: Published on 10 November 2026 - 10:38 GMT+1•Updated 10:43

Denmark is pouring another 500 million DKK (€66.9 million) into one of the world’s most powerful supercomputers, backed by pharmaceutical giant Novo Nordisk Foundation, under plans announced on Tuesday.
ADVERTISEMENT

The funding will support its supercomputer Gefion’s infrastructure and operations at the Danish Centre for AI Innovation (DCAI), which runs the machine, according to an announcement from the Export and Investment Fund of Denmark.
Further details of how the funding will be used and when the additional capacity will be available have not been revealed.
Denmark launched its supercomputer Gefion in 2024 with 1,528 Nvidia chips. The centre says it is now nearing full capacity.

The new investment adds to the initial 700 million DKK (€93.8 million) in funding from Denmark’s state investment fund and the Novo Nordisk Foundation, the Danish foundation behind the maker of weight-loss and diabetes drugs such as Ozempic.
‘New solutions, companies and jobs’
The aim is to turn greater access to computing power into economic growth.

“This gives Danish companies and researchers more computing power to translate good ideas into new solutions, companies and jobs,” said Martin Lidegaard, Denmark’s minister for business and competitiveness, in a statement.
“And it also strengthens our competitiveness, while ensuring that ownership of the technology of the future is not left to others,” he added.
Another aim is to help public institutions and businesses use AI while retaining control over sensitive data.

Netcompany, a Danish technology company that builds and operates public-sector IT systems, including for NHS England, is joining the centre’s investors. It will contribute software to manage access, monitoring and security.
What it means for Europe’s push for greater digital control
The announcement comes as European governments race to gain greater control over the infrastructure used to develop AI and the companies building it.
The United Kingdom invested £225 million (€269 million) in a supercomputer dedicated to AI research in 2023.
Meanwhile, Finland hosts a supercomputer, Large Unified Modern Infrastructure (LUMI), jointly funded by the European Union and participating countries at a lifetime cost of more than €200 million.

In July, the European Commission launched a call for up to seven AI gigafactories, larger data centres built to train and run advanced AI models, backed by up to €10 billion in European Union and national funding.

“Europe must be able to do much more itself, and Denmark must contribute to European technological independence — not least so that we can regulate and develop technology based on democratic values,” said Christina Egelund, Denmark’s minister for research, education and digitalisation.

items.titel: Portugal's last circus elephant adapts to life in new sanctuary, gaining 100kg
items.anriss: 'She can be in any habitat, she literally owns everything, she makes her own choices,' says the manager of the Pangea Sanctuary.

absaetze.t: After almost four months, Julie, the first resident of an elephant sanctuary created in the Alentejo, in southern Portugal, has begun to settle into her new home. It is an extensive enclosure that covers 400 hectares between Vila Viçosa and Alandroal, in the district of Évora.
ADVERTISEMENT

"Julie [when she arrived] was shy, it is like anyone who comes to a new place, who does not know anyone and does not know the surroundings. Slowly, about a week later, she began to trust and to decide what she wanted to go outside. There are many trails, so she has been tidying up the house and, in this case, making it her own home," said elephant keeper Johnny Nascimento, speaking to the Associated Press.

According to the Pangea sanctuary, Julie was the last circus elephant in Portugal and moved to the Alentejo in June after a voluntary agreement with the Victor Hugo Cardinali circus. Since then, she has already put on weight and can now move around as she pleases. One of her favourite pastimes is wallowing in mud pools.
'She has free access 24 hours a day'

"She has been with us for just over three months and has already gained about 100 kilos in that time, which is perfectly normal. Where she was before, she did not really have the opportunity to exercise, she was just in a shed most of the time. Whereas now she has free access 24 hours a day, she can be in the shelter, she can be in any habitat, she literally owns everything, she makes her own choices," explained Ryan Hockley, manager of the Pangea Sanctuary, to AP.
Julie was captured in Africa about 40 years ago. She arrived in Portugal when she was still very young and joined the Cardinali circus in 1988.
In 2018, Portugal banned wild animals from circuses, but the law only came into force in 2024, to give circuses time to adapt and find solutions for where to send the animals.

This is part of the reason behind the sanctuary, to be a new home for elephants in need coming from zoos, circuses and other places. It is estimated that there are more than 600 elephants in captivity across Europe.

"I think it is extremely important that someone has done what we are doing, that someone has created an elephant sanctuary. There are more than 600 elephants in Europe, Asian and African, and a proportion of those elephants are not in ideal conditions," lamented the head of the sanctuary.
'I think Portugal is the ideal choice'

The Portuguese region of the Alentejo was chosen for its warm climate, which can recreate conditions similar to those of the African continent. "If we were to choose anywhere in Europe, I think Portugal is the ideal choice, the climate gives me that feeling of being in Africa," said Hockley, drawing parallels between the Alentejo region and the landscapes of Tanzania or Kenya.
From now on, Pangea's goal is to keep expanding so that it can take in more animals in the future, with total capacity to house between 20 and 30 elephants.

"We are certainly the first large-scale elephant sanctuary in Europe, there is a sanctuary in France, but the enclosure they have is not as big as the one we have here, we have an incredible piece of land," he stressed in comments to AP.

Julie will not be alone for much longer. Another elephant from a circus in Belgium is expected to arrive at the sanctuary as early as November. Kariba, another African female, was also captured in the wild.

She should already have been transported to the sanctuary, but a series of infections prevented her from travelling safely. The animal had to be treated and only once all the conditions are in place will she be transported to Portugal.
For the time being, the sanctuary will remain closed to visitors, "providing Julie and future residents with the space and tranquillity they need to adapt".

items.titel: To Implement Acquisition Reform, Empower Military Mavericks
items.anriss: “I wanted disciplined but not regimented thinking. Commanders must encourage intellectual risk-taking to preclude a lethargic environment. Leaders must shelter those challenging nonconformists and mavericks who make institutions …

absaetze.t: “I wanted disciplined but not regimented thinking. Commanders must encourage intellectual risk-taking to preclude a lethargic environment. Leaders must shelter those challenging nonconformists and mavericks who make institutions uncomfortable; otherwise you wash out innovation.”
— James Mattis & Bing West, Call Sign Chaos

For the last decade, the Pentagon has had the authorities to buy commercially derived technologies at speed and scale, but not enough people who know how to use those authorities. Successive senior Pentagon leaders, both military and civilian, have asserted that these technologies will prove decisive in future wars. Panels, commissions, and directives created new pathways and the Pentagon’s Acquisition Transformation Strategy now makes commercial-first buying a top priority.

This article argues that the Defense Innovation Unit should lead the implementation of this transformation by becoming the department’s weapons school for commercial technology acquisition. Like the Navy and Air Force weapons schools, the unit should select promising servicemembers, train them rigorously, credential them visibly, and ultimately send them back to the services to lead and teach others. Two things make this work: training that turns motivated people into experts and incentives that ensure that time at the unit enhances their careers instead of ending them. The mavericks that built the unit had the first without the second, and many paid for it dearly.

Since 2016, the Defense Innovation Unit has executed hundreds of commercial solutions openings using other transaction agreements through partnerships with limited groups of service personnel whose acquisition knowledge has never scaled. The unit’s experience will be the bedrock of the curriculum.
Sign Up for Our Newsletter

In November 2014, then-Secretary of Defense Chuck Hagel announced that the Department of Defense was implementing a Third Offset Strategy in response to renewed Russian aggression in Eastern Europe and China’s militarization of the South China Sea. The strategy would “start with a clean sheet of paper” to field several commercially derived technologies, including robotics and autonomous systems. As a part of this strategy, Hagel’s successor, Secretary of Defense Ash Carter, announced that the Pentagon would be establishing a storefront in Silicon Valley called the Defense Innovation Unit Experimental.

In 2016, the unit’s three-person acquisition pathways team constructed a competitive solicitation process called a commercial solutions opening: a-three phase competition emphasizing speed, flexibility, and collaboration in the contracting process by using other transaction agreements, which played a prodigious role in winning the space race and had been re-invigorated by the 2016 National Defense Authorization Act. Using this process made the Pentagon a more appealing customer and leveled the playing field for startups by driving a commercial-friendly approach that recognized startups and their investors’ expectations by providing buy signals at the speed of business, not typical defense acquisition cycles.

From 2016 to 2024, the unit remained separated and secluded from the rest of the Pentagon. The unit had a modest budget, relying on motivated mission partners to fund projects. Servicemembers at the unit were mavericks whose intrinsic motivation to make an impact took precedence over promotion and advancement. They repeatedly warned the rest of the Pentagon about the threat of small drones to parked aircraft, the outsized role of drones in the Nagorno-Karabakh War, and the rapid proliferation of high-quality commercial satellite imagery. Despite complete alignment with the Third Offset Strategy, their warnings were routinely dismissed. While the unit punched well above its weight, it suffered budget cuts and spurious contract award protests.sustaining of spurious contract award protests In 2021, Director Mike Brown was nominated to be the Pentagon’s top acquisitions official, only to have his nomination derailed by unsubstantiated accusations of abusing hiring authorities. These events led many at the unit to perceive themselves as rebels resisting bloated Pentagon bureaucracy. Many servicemembers were shuffled back to the services where their careers were negatively impacted. One of us served as the unit’s first warfighter-in-residence, arriving ecstatic at the opportunity to make an impact on capabilities for his community. While many projects worked on were successful, it also meant permanently derailing the author’s military career.

Some of the unit’s most successful projects, including Persistent Maritime Intelligence, Surveillance, and Reconnaissance, Construction Scale Additive Manufacturing, and Peacetime Indications and Warning, came from coincidental alignment between funded mission problems and solutions from vendors like SailDrone, ICON Technology, Capella Space, and others whose founders hadn’t imagined the military as a customer.
In February 2022, imagery from Capella’s satellites showed the world that Russia was about to invade Ukraine.

After Russia invaded Ukraine, the unit’s mission was gradually legitimized by the prodigious impact of agile software development, small drones, and space-based sensing in the war. While some leaders openly demeaned the unit and commercial technology, others started to recognize the value of the commercial technologies emphasized by the Third Offset Strategy. Under the leadership of House Appropriations Defense Subcommittee Chairman Ken Calvert, congressional staffer Nathan Diller, and Calvert’s National Security Advisor, Michael MacKay, the unit’s director was codified as a principal staff assistant to the secretary of defense, appropriated an annual budget of almost $1 billion, and charged with creating “asymmetric advantage to support combatant command operational challenges.”

These new authorities and funding, which one of us strongly advocated for in War on The Rocks, empowered the unit to validate and accelerate privately-funded, commercial solutions to the military’s most urgent problems. In 2024, the unit solicited proposals for small, unmanned surface vessels that could strike enemy forces and low-cost cruise missiles. The first project led to Saronic Technologies receiving a $392 million contract for vessels that have since been used to rescue downed pilots and strike an Iranian submarine. The second project awarded agreements to Zone 5 Technologies and Anduril Industries and is now a program of record with the Air Force.

Since January 2025, the Pentagon has made three announcements marking a new era for the Defense Innovation Unit. In March 2025, the Pentagon released a memo mandating “Commercial Solutions Opening and other transactions as the default solicitation and award approaches for acquiring capabilities under the [Software Acquisition Pathway].” In November 2025, an acquisition transformation strategy designated acquisitions as a warfighting function and the unit’s commercial-first buying practices as “the preferred acquisition approach.” In January, a third memo recognized the unit as “the Department’s center of excellence for commercial technology adoption and product transition, available to Portfolio Acquisition Executives and program offices across the Department.”

Yet the Pentagon’s response to this competency gap places renewed responsibility on the institution that has long been responsible for closing it. The Acquisition Transformation Strategy calls for transforming the Defense Acquisition University into the Warfighting Acquisition University to produce tougher, faster buyers. The ambition is sound, but entrusting transformation to the same institutional training system requires more than a new name. Centralizing acquisition education and certification does not ensure that practitioners can construct and execute a program based on sound mission engineering, negotiate a commercially viable agreement, exercise judgment under uncertainty, or move a promising technology into operational use. Certification establishes a baseline, but it does not demonstrate mastery. The university’s success should be judged by whether graduates apply better buying practices and deliver better outcomes.

The services remain responsible for those outcomes, yet should use their own discretionary resources to address practical training gaps that centralized instruction leaves unresolved. That separates responsibility for workforce preparation from accountability for mission delivery. The answer is to give the services a stronger role in developing acquisition judgment through live work, supported by experienced government and industry practitioners. Other transaction agreements illustrate the need: Knowing the authority exists is different from structuring, negotiating, and executing an agreement that attracts a commercial company and meets a warfighter’s need. The Defense Innovation Unit can connect those two forms of learning by developing practitioners through actual acquisitions and returning them to the services prepared to execute and teach. Centralized education should support that pipeline, not substitute for it.

Instead of operating as a national missions force for innovation, the unit should position itself as the department’s weapons school for commercial technology acquisition. Military weapons schools, such as the U.S. Navy’s Top Gun and the U.S. Air Force Weapons School, are centers of excellence that maintain the highest standards of performance in their respective communities and facilitate disciplined, rigorous training by selecting promising pilots, aircrew, and support personnel from the operational forces and putting them through a comprehensive program that teaches them to be experts in their respective professions. Upon completion, they are given a weapons school patch that they wear for the rest of their career. Graduates are expected to both maintain the highest standards and teach others how to achieve those standards.

This analogy is particularly potent for three reasons. First, while weapons schools maintain their own cultures, standards, and unrivaled appetites for excellence, they are equally eager to teach others to achieve those standards. Second, weapons schools have prerequisites. The elite few students selected to attend arrive with operational experience, leave with a deeper knowledge and understanding of their craft, and return to lead by example and teach what they learned. Third, weapons schools are expected to hold their communities’ leaders accountable, even if that means disagreeing with general and flag officers.
To meet the moment, the unit should undertake a six-step process.
Select for Temperament and Reputation

The unit should seek out mavericks with reputations for challenging status quos and finding novel paths through institutional obstacles while following the law, including contracting officers that have awarded commercial contracts and operators that have shown initiative by identifying and sourcing solutions to their communities’ mission problems, with both commissioned and non-commissioned officers eligible for selection. The unit’s most experienced program managers and agreements officers should conduct candidate interviews and selections.
Run a Course, Not An Onboarding

items.titel: Winning Time: Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces and the New Dimension of War
items.anriss: In late 2023, Ukraine’s military leadership faced an institutional choice: establish a dedicated branch of the armed forces for unmanned systems or integrate drones into existing branches. Most senior officers I knew opposed the separate …

absaetze.t: In late 2023, Ukraine’s military leadership faced an institutional choice: establish a dedicated branch of the armed forces for unmanned systems or integrate drones into existing branches. Most senior officers I knew opposed the separate force, and their strongest argument was sound within classical doctrine. Each branch of service corresponds to a distinct domain of war: The army fights on land, the navy at sea, the air force in the air. Unmanned systems operate across all of these domains and possess none of their own. No domain, no branch of service. The advocates were mostly newcomers from civilian life, and the opponents were career generals. Within the coordinate system of existing doctrine, the generals were right. The war itself, however, was about to overtake their premise that it unfolds in fixed places. Ukraine created the Unmanned Systems Forces anyway, the first branch of its kind in the world. A force with about 2.5 percent of Ukraine’s military personnel has accounted for roughly a third of Russian losses this past year.

That decision reflected a collision of two cultures. People who entered from civilian life built a different culture: continuous experimentation in place of pre-defined standards and protocols, openness to mistakes as the price of learning, and the habit of improving weapons in combat. For career officers, the question was usually one of means: which systems, in what quantity, and for which branch. The real question lies elsewhere: What game are we playing, and how do we imagine it?

The decisive dimension of the war in Ukraine is not where forces fight, but how fast each side adapts. A unit that updates its tactics and technology every six weeks does not cancel the firepower of a unit that updates once a year — a slower side can still pay in mass, as Russia does. What the faster unit wins is time: It sets the terms of every exchange for as long as the gap lasts. Mass decides how long a side can continue to pay, and speed determines how much each payment buys. I call this the Time Domain: a competition not for territory but for time itself — the interval between the moment a new capability reaches the front and the point at which the enemy’s answer to it works — won by whoever adapts faster. It is also an answer to the generals: The Unmanned Systems Forces do have a battleground of their own — not a place on the map, but a contest, the one their machines are built to win faster than anyone else.

When Russia launched its full-scale invasion, I returned to Ukraine from Stanford to help its fight. I worked inside Aerorozvidka, the volunteer community that pioneered network-centric warfare in Ukraine and helped create the Delta battlefield management system around a single conviction: push battlefield information outward, to those who act on it, instead of holding it inside headquarters. Later, I advised the first commander of the Unmanned Systems Forces and built the team that created the 412th Brigade “Nemesis.”

Throughout this war, Russia has held superiority across every parameter a classical analyst would measure: personnel, artillery, missiles, armor. Under that asymmetry, innovation speed was never an advantage for Ukraine. It was a condition of existence.

The best commanders I worked with understood this intuitively: Tactics had to change faster, commanders had to build units differently, and time was the decisive resource. But they had no language to explain it to headquarters, no metric for a manufacturer, no concept to make it a requirement for doctrine. The analytical apparatus of military thought describes who stands where and how much each side has. It has no category for how quickly a force is becoming something else.

Military doctrine treats a domain as the environment in which operations take place, and NATO recognizes five: land, sea, air, cyberspace, and space. Each answers the question of “where.” But consider an ordinary grass field. People can play football, field hockey, and rugby on the same ground. The ground is identical, yet each game has its own team, its own rules, its own way of winning. The field does not define the game — the rules do. The pattern holds here, too: a distinct game with its own objective and rules, one a force wins on its own terms. Cyberspace earned its spot on the list not because it occupies a physical location, but because the contest there follows a logic the older categories never captured. This is what happened with Ukraine’s drone units. On that shared field, they were playing by rules nobody had written down, and they created a new game: a technology race detached from any portion of space, yet decisive in what happens on the ground. That is the game Ukraine built the Unmanned Systems Forces to play. American author Edward Luttwak described the search for a response as inherent in any military interaction: Adversaries constantly work to reverse each other’s moves. Every advantage has an expiry date. The only question is who renews it first. A single metric judges any decision, whether a commander’s, an engineer’s, or a procurement official’s, by how much time it buys before the enemy adapts.

None of this will satisfy a reader schooled in classical doctrine, and the objection is worth stating at full strength. Adaptation speed, how it runs, is not an environment but an attribute of every competition — present across all five domains rather than forming a sixth beside them. Cyberspace at least offered networks and hardware to stand in for terrain. But terrain was never what earned cyberspace its place — a lattice that rebuilds itself daily makes poor geography. NATO’s own doctrine has moved the same way: Since 2022, it has defined an “operational domain” not as a piece of the physical world but as “a specified sphere of capabilities and activities that can be applied within an engagement space” — the environment shapes each one, but none equals it. What makes this a domain of war, and not the truism that innovation matters everywhere, is the prize.

What adversaries contest in each defines every category: ground, sea lanes, the air, the flow of information, orbit. Logistics, command, and morale run through all five and adversaries attack them in each, yet no one classifies them as domains, because none of them is a prize — they are a way to play for prizes that lie elsewhere. Adaptation speed, taken alone, is also a way of playing. Time is not. The interval between a move and the enemy’s working answer is measurable. A force spends it, and it compounds, and no other domain holds it as its objective. The defender who trades space for time buys hours inside a fixed set of tactics and systems. The real contest, instead, concerns the weeks it takes to keep that set ahead of the enemy’s. A prize needs an owner, and an operational category is that assignment of responsibility, carrying its own doctrine, command, and budget. Treat the contest for time as an attribute of the others, and it becomes everyone’s concern and no one’s mission. Treat it as distinct, and command charges someone with winning it. Ukraine already has.

That is what the label buys in practice: a mandate and a frame. The Unmanned Systems Forces exist to win time. This operational sphere gives them an objective of their own on the battlefield, a way of measuring it, and their own means of pursuing it. Every decision the force makes — what to buy, how to train, how to fight — stands or falls on whether it wins time.

Tempo and operational speed describe how fast you execute within an existing framework of tactics and systems. The Time Domain is the contest over how fast the framework itself changes. That its prize plays out within the other domains does not place it above them: Air superiority registers on the ground, and no one denies that the air is its own contest. John Boyd taught that victory belongs to whoever operates inside the opponent’s decision cycle. The war in Ukraine has extended his insight from the individual engagement to the entire military organism, from observation through engineering and production, and back into combat.

The window between a new system appearing at the front and an effective enemy counter sometimes lasts only weeks. That compression is what is new. Armies have always adapted, and every advantage has always expired. But while a cycle spanning years could leave the branches fighting in each domain a cycle measured in weeks cannot: The interval itself becomes the contest, and a contest needs an owner on the battlefield.

Russia plays this game, too, and sometimes plays it well. It was first to field jam-proof fiber-optic drones at scale, using them to devastating effect around Kursk and forcing Ukraine into a catch-up cycle of its own. Russia had no branch then, but it had Rubicon, a defense-ministry center that runs developers, staff officers, and operators in one loop, following logic similar to that of the Combat Hub. The lead it won lasted months. By April 2025, Ukraine had more than 20 certified fiber-optic models from 11 producers, and the race was on again. Moscow then followed Ukraine’s logic to the end: In December 2024, Putin ordered a branch of his own, and by late 2025 Russia’s Unmanned Systems Forces were operational, down to the name. The adversary copied the form because it works — proof that anyone can win a round, but the victor is whoever owns the form.

Nor is the game confined to our theater. In the Red Sea, the Houthis escalated within months from drones and land-attack cruise missiles to anti-ship cruise and ballistic missiles with far shorter reaction times, and the U.S. Navy rewrote its tactics as they did. By the end of 2025, U.S. Central Command had fielded a one-way attack drone of its own, modeled, in its own words, on Iran’s Shahed. When the world’s most powerful military copies its adversary’s weapon to close an adaptation gap, the Time Domain is no longer a Ukrainian curiosity.

The clearest place to see this game institutionalized is the 412th Brigade “Nemesis” — the example I know best. It grew out of a project centered on a single system — a strike copter whose first models carried about six kilograms over 10 kilometers, and whose latest versions can reach nearly 100. In the project’s first seven months, 47 crews flew over 950 combat sorties and destroyed more than 520 targets, including over 360 pieces of equipment valued at $308 million. The price was 107 airframes lost, worth about $3.2 million — roughly a hundred dollars of destroyed Russian equipment for every dollar of airframe lost. These figures come from the project’s own flight records rather than from any public dataset. I use them as primary material.

In December 2023, the project spun off a separate experimental battalion, and the clearest gain was temporal: The loop between manufacturer and frontline shortened. In under two years, the battalion grew into a regiment and then a brigade. Its structure now includes a dedicated technology and innovation unit. Its analytical section studies everything from sortie rates to munitions effectiveness, and its academy trains pilots and engineers at its own base. This is a new type of combat unit, with its own research, production, and school, whose product is the speed of its own evolution as much as any individual strike.

The pattern extends beyond one brigade and one branch. Lasar’s Group, a Ukrainian National Guard unit credited with destroying $12 billion worth of Russian equipment, built the same architecture from a different starting point: It began in 2022 as a volunteer team building its first drones at its own expense, without state funding. No one ordered this design into being. It emerged on its own, evolved independently, and reproduces itself because it solves a real problem of war.

items.titel: The Enduring Genius of Janet Malcolm
items.anriss: By the time I learned who Janet Malcolm was, it turned out that I had been circling her for some time. What I mean is that I had known about her work—I had read some of her articles in college classes and for pleasure, had had her books …

absaetze.t: By the time I learned who Janet Malcolm was, it turned out that I had been circling her for some time. What I mean is that I had known about her work—I had read some of her articles in college classes and for pleasure, had had her books recommended to me by more than one beloved professor—but I just never had any reason to note the byline. If you are among those in the know, this may sound ridiculous to you. When you know of Janet Malcolm you spot traces of her everywhere. You understand that she was a titan of American letters—a longtime staff writer for The New Yorker, a member of the American Academy of Arts and Letters, a National Book Award finalist, and the list goes on. You register her far-reaching influence. You can see that she was running circles around everyone else. But if you don’t know to look for her name, it is easy to miss.
Article continues after advertisement

This was by design. To say that Malcolm was disinterested in being a celebrity is an understatement. She was actively opposed to the idea. While other prominent writers in her milieu—Susan Sontag, Joan Didion, Renata Adler—became recognizable names and faces, the literary It Girls of their day, Malcolm generally did what she could to stay out of view. She didn’t like to talk about her work. She almost never posed for photos, sat for interviews, or did readings. When she and Didion both celebrated their eightieth birthdays in 2014, New York Magazine wanted to run a joint tribute, and Malcolm said no. Even for a rare appearance, a live conversation in 2012 with the writer Katie Roiphe at NYU for The Paris Review, she insisted on reading a pre-written interview transcript aloud rather than speaking off the cuff. “There was something sublime and deranged about this arrangement,” Roiphe later wrote of the event, “but there was also an elegance to her solution: She had found a way to be both present and not, at the same time.”
Above all, she was fixated on the realities of a writer’s subjectivity long before it was commonplace or fashionable for journalists to interrogate the limits of their own perspective.

There are a number of possible explanations for Malcom’s notorious reticence. A woman, a Jew, and an émigré, she was always a member of the minority, though she didn’t dwell on it. She was also a late bloomer: She didn’t publish her first piece of reported long-form journalism, the kind of writing for which she would become known, until 1978, when she was forty-three years old. And then in 1984, Jeffrey Masson, a Sanskrit scholar, a psychoanalyst, and the subject of Malcolm’s In the Freud Archives, sued her for libel, tarnishing her image even though she eventually won the suit. Concurrent to the legal battle—which lasted over a decade, all in—Malcolm published The Journalist and the Murderer, a long piece of reporting about another journalist who was sued by a subject. The opening sentence of Malcolm’s piece—“Every journalist who is not too stupid or too full of himself to notice what is going on knows that what he does is morally indefensible”—quickly became one of journalism’s most controversial and oft-quoted lines (a reviewer once referred to it as Malcolm’s Law). Her peers went berserk, both because she had come for their profession and because she had neglected, at first, to acknowledge the obvious overlap between her choice of subject and the events of her own life. They called her a tattler, a backstabber, a cop, “journalism’s school slut.” As soon as she was able, Malcolm retreated from the public eye.

But she never stopped writing. In fact, the years when Malcolm was facing Masson in court and taking a beating from members of her profession in the pages of their publications were the most productive years of her writing life. She profiled artists, wrote laser-focused criticism of books and photography, and published multiple long-form journalistic pieces that would come to be recognized as exemplars of the genre. Her work shared some DNA with the New Journalists, who used literary techniques such as inserting themselves into their work to write nonfiction as vivid as fiction, but went somewhere else entirely. Thanks, perhaps to a long-standing interest in psychoanalysis, she was intensely focused on the inner lives of her subjects, the psychological dynamics playing out in the scenes she witnessed, and the morality of the work she was doing.

Above all, she was fixated on the realities of a writer’s subjectivity long before it was commonplace or fashionable for journalists to interrogate the limits of their own perspective. Regardless of the subject, each piece she wrote was also an examination of how people tell stories—about themselves and on behalf of others—and of the ethical morass of any act of narrativizing. In her writing, she explored these questions with a provocative sure-footedness that made her easy to criticize during the years she was taking the stand, and a hero to many—a true writer’s writer—in the decades that followed.

When I first became properly aware of Malcolm in 2018, this thorny metacommentary was a source of intrigue. She was there but not there, famous but also shrouded in mystery. At the time I was a student at Yale University, fascinated by journalism, Freudians, and the detritus of other people’s lives—three varyingly niche interests I shared, as it turns out, with Malcolm. In 2013, she had sold her papers to Yale’s Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library. But when I started studying them five years later, they were just being opened to the public, making me one of the first people to spend time in the Janet Malcolm archive.

Each day that year, I descended into the library’s subterranean reading room—a place Malcolm also spent time in the early 2000s while working on a book about Alice B. Toklas and Gertrude Stein—to sift through the contents of another messy box of her papers. I learned to read her handwriting with ease and grew familiar with the turns of phrase she would use in short faxes to friends or the stern tone she would take when an editor had gone against her wishes. Above all, I learned to be patient while examining overfilled boxes of messy, confusing, repetitive, and frequently boring papers.
Accordingly, Malcolm acolytes will tell you that she is everywhere and nowhere within her work.

Much of the materials—which Malcom had prepared for their sale to Yale—seemed, at first, to pertain strictly to business. But the more time I spent in the archive, the more her personal life started to seep in around the edges. I found official documents from her childhood—Czech papers, her certification of American Citizenship, her middle-school report cord, stowed in an unsuspecting envelope between thick folders of miscellaneous correspondence. I stumbled on carefully typed instructions for the house sitter about how to adequately look after her prized plants and cats. I began to see how draft upon draft of the same page or paragraph (Malcom would frequently try writing out a passage four or five different ways in order to even start to get it right) tells a story of the writer at work.

Above all, I became obsessed with the letters. Malcolm understood the appeal: “Only when he reads a subject’s letters does the biographer feel he has come fully into his presence,” she once wrote. As with the rest of her papers, much of the correspondence in Malcolm’s archive was nominally about work. But even letters exchanged with a peer or editor contained moments of quiet revelation. While she appears in her published writing as a terrifyingly sharp, often dispassionate observer of other people—one critic wrote of her journalism, “Not content simply to tell her subjects’ stories, she believes it is a writer’s responsibility to judge them”—notes to and from sources reveal her humanity.

She was genial. She was interested in her subjects’ day-to-day lives. She cared deeply about what they thought of her writing while also recognizing that she couldn’t control their reactions. Though she wrote at length about the fraught ethics of the journalist-subject relationship, she could get beyond it: It was not uncommon for her to stay in touch with people after she was done writing about them. Some even became good friends.

My experience of combing Malcolm’s archive was as intimate as it was unsettling. I grew fiercely attached to her while working on a project that I sensed she would not be happy about. Much of Malcolm’s writing touches on the strange voyeurism and uncanny attachments that develop when you’re writing about someone else. “Biographical research leads to a kind of insufferable familiarity,” she once observed in an essay about the Bloomsbury Group. Or, of the genre on the whole, “It is an unholy practice, the telling of a life story that isn’t one’s own on the basis of oppressively massive quantities of random, not necessarily reliable information.” Reading these words at night after a day spent poring over her drafts, letters, invoices, and assorted scribbles was at once funny and discomfiting. I could see, from my own experience doing the thing Malcolm purported to hate in her own archive, that she as almost certainly right.

Adding another layer of strangeness to the whole exercise was that Malcolm was, at the time, still alive and well, going about her life in New York City, and not just a disembodied voice on the page in my imagination. I just didn’t have access to her. Early on in my research, I had written to Malcolm asking if she would speak to me as part of the project for which she had become my subject. It should come as no surprise that she rebuffed my request. “I’m so sorry, but I must say no to your proposal of talking with me about my work,” she replied. “I just never do that. I feel my writing must speak for itself. As Isadora Duncan said, ‘If I could talk about it, I wouldn’t have to dance it.’ ” This was a version of the same response Malcolm gave to the vast majority of her would-be interviewers: The work speaks for itself. And if she’s not speaking, it also speaks for her. Okay, I figured, why not take her at her word? What does the work say about the writer behind it?

As in her archive, one must dig a little to find Malcolm in her own writing. Until the very end of her career, she almost entirely avoided writing squarely about herself. As she once remarked to a friend, “No, I don’t think I will ever do a book in which I have to do all the talking—too strenuous. “Even when she finally wrote a memoir in the last years of her life, she structured it around a series of family photographs, which she appraised with her characteristic degree of remove.

Accordingly, Malcolm acolytes will tell you that she is everywhere and nowhere within her work. She pops up or interjects when you least expect it: to mention her psychiatrist father in passing, to inquire after the well-being of a cat. The critic James Wood once tellingly said that she moves around her subjects “like a janitor at an orgy.” She regarded everyone with the same cutting, distanced gaze. But she didn’t exempt herself. Every piece she wrote about someone else—which is to say, nearly every piece she wrote—told two stories simultaneously: the story of the subjects, and the story, always fraught and often veiled, of her retelling.

For example, in The Silent Woman, her 1994 account of the writers jockeying to tell the story of Slyvia Plath, Malcolm lays out the uneasy positions of Plath’s many biographers, friends-turned-memoirists and even a former flame before revealing, some seventy pages in, her bias toward on in particular. “My narrative would be revisionist,” she wrote, implicating herself in the very problem—that is, the inability of any biographer to see her subject clearly—that she was diagnosing.

items.titel: My Electric Journey Out of Darkness: 10 Books on Electroconvulsive Therapy
items.anriss: Electroconvulsive therapy is often used as a last line of treatment against mood disorders. It works by sending short electrical shocks to the brain to induce a seizure. The approach was innovated in Italy, where they coined an efficient …

absaetze.t: Electroconvulsive therapy is often used as a last line of treatment against mood disorders. It works by sending short electrical shocks to the brain to induce a seizure. The approach was innovated in Italy, where they coined an efficient transitive verb to describe what the machine does to you: zapare, meaning “to zap.”

As a grateful zappee, I sometimes get the question: Why do so many writers get ECT? I’m not sure we do, really. I just think we’re more likely to write about it. The less-glib response would be that writers are often down to try the risqué, or to make experiments in our lives.

For a long time, I resisted writing anything about my experiences of getting voluntarily electrocuted, or about the touches of memory loss that followed. It didn’t seem the sort of thing one should crow about. But I kept getting maddening questions about the whole process. “Were they punishing you?” Or, “Isn’t that just a high-tech lobotomy?” Not at all. Along with music and true love, electroshock is one of the few real miracles I’ve experienced firsthand.

So I wrote a book about it, Jolt: My Electric Journey Out of Darkness. The title, I grant, is somewhat dramatic. But then the treatment itself offers an undeniable sense of drama: you lie down on a table, are given a euphoric cocktail of anesthetics and muscle relaxants, and—after the indicated number of treatments—you arise sufficiently changed that you no longer wish to disappear from life.

One early reader of Jolt, who receives semiregular maintenance ECT treatments, wrote to me the other week: “I remember an actual medical doctor saying to me just last year that he couldn’t believe ECT was ‘still a thing.’ It horrified me. I want to stuff Jolt into his hands. Maybe smack him around with it first. But then stuff it into his hands.” That’s a bit violent for my taste, but I certainly honor the sentiment.
Point being: books can offer a lifeline for patients. Here are some that offered one to me.
Sylvia Plath, The Bell Jar

I’ve long been confused to see Plath held up as a cautionary tale about ECT. In fact, Plath—like her novelistic stand-in, Esther—was saved by the treatment. It’s true that Esther’s first experience with unmodified shock therapy is traumatic:

…something bent down and took hold of me and shook me like the end of the world. Whee-ee-ee-ee-ee, it shrilled, through an air crackling with blue light, and with each flash a great jolt drubbed me till I thought my bones would break and the sap fly out of me like a split plant.
I wondered what terrible thing it was that I had done.

But once Esther enters the care of a far more sensible and kind doctor (a loosely fictionalized version of Plath’s own Dr. Ruth Barnhouse), she receives modified ECT, administered with an anesthetic and muscle relaxant. (“If It’s done properly,” Doctor Nolan said, “it’s like going to sleep.”) After her first modified treatment, Esther reports on the experience of anesthesia and awakening:

…darkness wiped me out like chalk on a blackboard….I woke out of a deep, drenched sleep…. All the heat and fear had purged itself. I felt surprisingly at peace. The bell jar hung, suspended, a few feet above my head. I was open to the circulating air.

Given that Esther was suicidal until this breakthrough, it’s a little odd to see Plath’s continued conscription into a chorus of ECT voices. In biographies, Plath was judged to have experienced long-term remission after her ECT course under Dr. Barnhouse. Just as salient, for me: if you read The Bell Jar, or anything else by Plath for that matter, you’ll see that ECT doesn’t doom creativity. (It’s the illness that does that.)
Edward Shorter and David Healy, Shock Therapy: A History of Electroconvulsive Treatment in Mental Illness

A crucial and thrilling history, merciless and evenhanded in its descriptions of the precursors of ECT (these include insulin coma therapy and metrazol shock treatment), and the authors cover the full range of its colorful history. In these pages, you’ll drop your jaw at the historical abuses of ECT—and you’ll wonder equally at the stunning success stories. The authors evoke the historical ironies with beautiful precision. Take the disputes between psychoanalysts and proponents of somatic treatments such as ECT:

For the analysts, ECT was a brutal, primitive treatment, sadistically inflicted, and masochistically accepted as an expiation of guilt. Yet behind the scenes many analysts were warmer toward ECT because they needed it to make their patients better….ECT, it could be said, was the secret love of psychoanalysis.
Shorter and Healy are also capable of something like poetry:

A major difference between Prozac and Zoloft compared with ECT is that these drugs come with the stamp of familiarity, whereas ECT for most people is quite alien. ECT is treated as a stranger; Prozac is treated as a neighbor.
A keenly balanced and richly informative account. Best to read once you’re on the mend.
Robert Pirsig, Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance

In the 1970s and ‘80s, Pirsig attained a priestly status among readers, and this big book became a counterculture scripture. The novel’s turning-point is when the narrator recalls being involuntarily subjected to ECT. As the narrator says of his former self:

[He was] destroyed by order of the court, enforced by the transmission of high-voltage alternating current through the lobes of his brain. Approximately 800 mills of amperage at durations of 0.5-1.5s had been applied on twenty-eight consecutive occasions, in a process known technologically as “Annihilation ECS.” A whole personality had been liquidated without a trace in a technologically faultless act….

Like The Bell Jar, Pirsig’s blockbuster philosophical novel (the narrator calls it a “chautauqua”) contains elements of autobiography. But its fictionalization of life is much looser than Plath’s. Still, many readers developed a parasocial love for the narrator—and grew furious on his behalf, to the extent that even today the novel is still sometimes invoked as a devastating indictment of electroshock. Yet the main character’s electroshock has very little to do with Pirsig’s own experience. As David Healy and Bruce G. Charlton observed in 2009, in the journal Medical Hypotheses:

…newly published biographical information on Pirsig from Mark Richardson (Zen and Now: On the Trail of Robert Pirsig and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance, New York: Knopf; 2008) has documented that the role of ECT in ZAMM is a “literary device,” added at a late stage in drafting the book. In reality the ECT had erased some short-term memory, but Pirsig’s long-term memory had quickly returned….It seems that one of the most famous depictions of ECT, one that had appeared factual, was actually fictional.

As literary devices go, it’s a brilliant one: the long-delayed smoking gun in the narrator’s quest to unravel the mystery of what happened to him. The book’s narrator is so engaging, and Pirsig’s own style so appealing, that one can almost forgive his acolytes for their overdetermined loyalty to his fictional counterpart.
Donald Antrim, One Friday in April
As Donald Antrim writes in this remarkable account of depression and deliverance, it was David Foster Wallace who persuaded him to seek out ECT. Antrim recounts the near-miraculous results:

We talk about the weight of the world. After ECT, the feeling in my body of immense weight went away; I felt a kind of physical lightness….These days I think of ECT as clean power, good electricity added to a wet, saline medium in which electrical signaling has become chaotic and mistimed.
ECT, of course, remains stigmatized, and Antrim memorably refers to stigma as “society’s unacknowledged violence toward the sick.” In One Friday, the author does noble work to counter that violence.
Martha Manning, Undercurrents: A Therapist’s Reckoning with Depression

Manning is a delight on the page (and reportedly in person), whether she’s discussing childcare or mental illness. And her lucid remarks about the ECT that delivered her from unbearable depression felt, to me, like light belatedly allowed into a horrible container where I’d been confined:

Nobody bats an eye when electricity is delivered to a stalled heart. There is no outcry. In fact, it’s considered a miracle….I will never be the ECT poster-girl. I am the first to admit the downside—confusion and memory loss. But damn it, it worked. I didn’t want to have it. Who would? I didn’t want to have a caesarian section either. I ended up with a terrible infection, a long scar, and a difficult recovery. But I got Keara. A beautiful healthy new life….I’d do it again in a heartbeat….In choosing the hospital and ECT I chose to fight for my life.
Camilla Nord, The Balanced Brain: The Science of Mental Health

Nord is a neuroscientist and an excellent translator of complicated science for a broad popular audience. Among her many fascinations is neurogenesis: the brain’s capacity for growth and self-renewal. Antipsychiatry voices, particularly anti-ECT partisans, like to describe ECT as causing “brain damage.” From the neuroscientists with whom I’ve spoken, that’s utterly wrong. Taken most generously, that critique confuses disruption with damage. Among its innumerable insights, The Balanced Brain, offers a fascinating reading of the hippocampal growth often spurred by a successful course of electroshock: “On balance, rather than brain death, ECT may be more likely to engender brain cell life.”
Carrie Fisher, Wishful Drinking and Shockaholic

I read Fisher’s memoirs before my electro-treatments. Her writing prepared me for localized memory loss—and implicitly reassured me about many other things, including one’s ability to retain a sense of humor, even after a deep disturbance and the shock that restores equanimity. Fisher is quite breezy about her memory loss, writing that she’s learned “to live in the present, now that the past seems to be otherwise engaged.” I’m blessed to have lost far less memory than Fisher did. (While I got a lot of treatments—23 in all, over the course of a few months—Fisher received many more over the course of years.) Tellingly, not once does she suggest that these memory deficits were debilitating; nor that they weren’t absolutely worth it.
Charles Fernyhough, Pieces of Light: The New Science of Memory

Completely reframed my way of thinking about autonoetic consciousness—i.e. the proprietary sense of your memories as belonging to a single self. “Memory is an artist as much as it is a scientist,” Fernyhough writes. As I went about rediscovering certain lost memories, and making peace with the unrecoverable ones, this sharp and compassionate book was an enormous help and comfort.
A. Alvarez, The Savage God: A Study of Suicide

Kay Redfield Jamison has called this singular 1971 study “rather romantic.” I suppose it is. But along with Jamison’s Night Falls Fast: Understanding Suicide, it’s one of the best books on the topic. Richly psychoanalytic, deeply literary, unflinchingly personal. It helped me understand the chillingly rational part of me that had craved a release from life. And I needed to understand that part fully before I was able to free myself of it. There were many people and things that called me back, including friends and family, as well as ECT—and this book.
Jolt: My Electric Journey Out of Darkness by Ted Scheinman is available from Scribner, an imprint of Simon & Schuster.

items.titel: Au musée de la Marine, comment l’humanité a exploré les abysses depuis l’Antiquité
items.anriss: De scaphandres en sous-marins, de monstres en œuvres d’art, l’exposition « L’Appel des profondeurs » retrace au musée national de la Marine, à Paris, des siècles d’exploration des fonds marins. Plongez dans une histoire à couper le souffle …

absaetze.t: L’accueil met tout de suite dans le bain ! Une raie fossilisée, découverte au sommet d’une montagne libanaise, ouvre le parcours de l’exposition « L’Appel des profondeurs », présentée au musée national de la Marine, à Paris. La preuve que le sol que l’on piétine fut un jour couvert d’eau : de quoi donner le vertige dès les premiers pas.

Autour du spécimen marin, les commissaires Louise Contant et Clémence Laurent ont réuni quelque 280 pièces, pour immerger les visiteurs au cœur d’une obsession humaine millénaire : sous l’eau, qu’y a-t-il ?
Le rêve des grands fonds

La première motivation pour explorer le royaume du silence est commerciale. Des perles fines du golfe Arabo-Persique au corail rouge, en passant par le murex dont Tyr tire sa pourpre, les plongeurs en apnée vont remonter des trésors depuis les fonds marins, quitte à tarir des bancs entiers d’huîtres, comme au large du Venezuela au XVIe siècle. Longtemps, l’imagination est au pouvoir et les cartes marines grouillent de bêtes féroces. On le constate même dans le « sérieux » traité sur les poissons du médecin Guillaume Rondelet qui n’hésite pas à y glisser un monstre en robe de moine. Alexandre le Grand serait descendu dans un tonneau de verre ? La légende coule des jours heureux.
Une créativité débordante

Au XIXe siècle, les avancées techniques affluent et tout s’accélère. Pour poser les premiers câbles télégraphiques, il faut sonder les fonds. Un jour, on en remonte un couvert de coraux à plus de 2 000 mètres : la vie existe bien ici-bas ! Les expéditions s’enchaînent, notamment celle de Challenger qui rapporte des milliers d’échantillons et laisse son nom à la fosse la plus profonde du globe. On innove aussi à tout-va, en particulier avec le scaphandre à casque de cuivre. Le médecin Paul Bert décrypte la décompression pour limiter les accidents, et des peintres embarquent pour croquer sur le vif des créatures qui perdent leurs couleurs dès qu’elles quittent leur milieu naturel.

En 1898, Louis Boutan plonge avec son appareil photo enfermé dans un caisson étanche et rapporte les premières images sous-marines. Les planches d’Ernst Haeckel [ill. en une] fertilisent tout un imaginaire, des visions sur papier du symboliste Odilon Redon aux formes de l’Art nouveau, de méduses en anémones. Le public en raffole et se presse dans les aquariums : « C’est vraiment une révolution de regard », résume Louise Contant.
Des sous-marins jaunes dans le grand bleu

Au XXe siècle, on va encore plus loin. « C’est le règne de l’homme-poisson », sourit la commissaire Clémence Laurent. Notamment parce qu’en 1943, le détendeur de Cousteau et Gagnan permet de couper le tuyau qui reliait le plongeur à la surface. Avec les palmes, on se rêve en sirènes des temps modernes – ce que ne manque pas d’immortaliser Marc Chagall.

Plus concrètement, certains repoussent les limites, comme la bathysphère qui dépasse les 900 mètres dans les années 1930 ou le Trieste touchant en 1960 le point le plus bas du globe, à 10 916 mètres. En 1977, c’est au tour du submersible Alvin de mettre en évidence des cheminées hydrothermales grouillantes de vie, sans une once de soleil. La cartographe Marie Tharp, elle, dessine le relief du plancher océanique et vient confirmer la dérive des continents. La pop culture fraye dans ces eaux-là, du Yellow Submarine des Beatles au Grand Bleu, pendant que les sous-marins nucléaires et les forages pétroliers font des abysses un terrain stratégique.

L’art contemporain, très présent dans les dernières salles, fait naturellement écho à cette conquête des fonds marins. Laure Prouvost transforme en vitrail le Rêve de la femme du pêcheur d’Hokusai, quand Marc Johnson tisse Return, tapisserie d’un bleu profond qui évoque la mémoire de la traite atlantique. La Koweïtienne Monira Al Qadiri, issue d’un pays pétrolier, expose une tête de forage brisée et côtoie les photos de fonds brumeux de Jonàs Forchini dans la zone industrielle de Fos-sur-Mer.
Un écosystème fragile

« Moins de 1 % des fonds marins a été observé visuellement et seuls 20 % ont été cartographiés ; la Lune est mieux connue que nos océans », rappellent les commissaires, alors que l’eau recouvre aujourd’hui les trois quarts de la surface du globe et constitue « 99 % de l’espace vital de la planète en volume ».

Pour répondre aux industriels qui lorgnent sur les plaines abyssales, le plasticien suisse Julian Charrière a immergé une lentille de phare dans le noir du Pacifique, au-dessus d’une de ces zones convoitées. Pas un seul humain à bord, juste un faisceau autour duquel des poissons rayonnent, tourbillonnent. D’une beauté insondable…

items.titel: Dans 'deux couteaux', le poète Vincent Annen fait le portrait en vers de son père
items.anriss: Lauréat du prix de poésie C.F. Ramuz 2025 et récemment couronné du Prix Rimbaud 2026 avec son recueil 'deux couteaux', le jeune poète romand Vincent Annen livre une déclaration d'amour ciselée à son père, ouvrier d'usine dans les …

absaetze.t: Lauréat du prix de poésie C.F. Ramuz 2025 et récemment couronné du Prix Rimbaud 2026 avec son recueil 'deux couteaux', le jeune poète romand Vincent Annen livre une déclaration d'amour ciselée à son père, ouvrier d'usine dans les abattoirs et cueilleur de champignons passionné.
S'il a deux couteaux, le père de Vincent, c'est parce qu'avec l'un il tue et découpe les animaux à la chaîne, et avec l'autre, dans les sous-bois, il prélève délicatement des champignons.
"se plier tenir dans une poche, discretça s’appelle comme ça, je croiscouteau de pochel’autre je ne sais pas, couteau de gorge, peut-être"
Extrait de 'deux couteaux' de Vincent Annen

Dans ce poème composé en sept parties autour d'un centre intitulé 'le héros', Vincent Annen dit le dur labeur d'un paternel dont la plus grande partie des journées est passée à se servir d'une lame afin d'ôter la vie et la débiter pour en faire des morceaux de viande à consommer sous vide. C'est avec les yeux de l'enfant que l'auteur, entré à présent dans la trentaine, approche ce minotaure, grand boiteux, aux bras "très très gros", et aux deux yeux "pas sûr de la couleur", dans lesquels il y a "d'autres yeux qui se ferment".
La poésie de mondes contrastés

Sujet rare en littérature, et d'autant plus précieux, le texte du jeune Broyard a une portée quasi politique. Le métier du père est imprimé dans son corps, le fils en saisit les marques et les imprime dans un texte. Les mondes extrêmement contrastés de ce père deviennent rythme, sonorité, et constituent désormais la musicalité d'un poème intitulé 'deux couteaux'.
J'avais une matière absolument formidable sous les yeux... et presque étrangère pour la plupart des gens

Restituer l'intime, le familial de façon si directe a représenté pour l'auteur un défi dont il s'était jusqu'ici tenu à l'écart. La matière riche à disposition a eu raison de son hésitation. Ce troisième recueil étoffe encore un peu plus son talent de poète.

Tendre et sans concession, l'auteur parvient, de façon délicate et magistrale, à nous faire ressentir toute la complexité qui accompagne l'acte de raconter au plus près de leur vérité les êtres qui nous sont chers. Le père de Vincent Annen ne se mesure évidemment pas aux lames des deux couteaux, mais émerge assurément de la pointe de la plume de son fils.
"papa il a bien plus que deux,papa il est"
